title: Why China can't fix its broken economy

scenes.say: China's economy grew 4.5 per cent last quarter.
scenes.speak: China's economy grew four and a half per cent last quarter.

scenes.say: On paper, that's fine.
But underneath is a problem Beijing can't fix: Chinese people aren't spending enough.
Why China can't fix its broken economy.
scenes.title: Why China can't fix its broken economy

scenes.say: Consumption makes up only about 56 per cent of China's economy.
scenes.title: Consumption in China
scenes.speak: Consumption makes up only about fifty-six per cent of China's economy.

scenes.say: In most economies, it's 70 per cent or more.
scenes.speak: In most economies, it's seventy per cent or more.

scenes.say: That's about 10 points below Japan in the 1990s, at the worst of its lost decade.
scenes.text: Below Japan | in its lost decade
scenes.speak: That's about ten points below Japan in the nineteen-nineties, at the worst of its lost decade.

scenes.say: No major economy in 100 years has spent so little of what it makes.
scenes.speak: No major economy in a hundred years has spent so little of what it makes.

scenes.say: Why does it matter? Because low spending is a warning light.
The model that built China's rise, build, invest, export, is running out of road.
scenes.text: Build. Invest. Export. | Running out of road.

scenes.say: Growth topped 10 per cent in the early 2000s. This spring, it hit a three-year low.
scenes.title: From double digits to under 5%
scenes.speak: Growth topped ten per cent in the early two-thousands. This spring, it hit a three-year low.

scenes.say: And debt has climbed to alarming levels.
Factories are humming: manufacturing grew 5.9 per cent. Retail sales? Just 1.1.
scenes.speak: Factories are humming: manufacturing grew five point nine per cent. Retail sales? Just one point one.

scenes.say: The factories are running. The shoppers are not.
Consumer prices rose just 0.9 per cent in September. Barely any inflation, because barely any demand.
scenes.speak: Consumer prices rose just zero point nine per cent in September. Barely any inflation, because barely any demand.

scenes.say: The biggest drag is housing, where Chinese families kept their savings.
Property investment fell 20.6 per cent this year.
scenes.label: Real-estate investment, January to September 2026
scenes.speak: Property investment fell twenty point six per cent this year.

scenes.say: Construction is shrinking. Home prices in the big cities are still lower than a year ago.
Overall investment in cities fell 7.2 per cent.
scenes.label: Urban fixed-asset investment, January to September 2026
scenes.speak: Overall investment in cities fell seven point two per cent.

scenes.say: When your flat loses value, you feel poorer. You save more. You spend less.
scenes.text: Feel poorer. | Save more. | Spend less.

scenes.say: And that deepens the slump.
But China can't just make less. That would mean mass layoffs.
So the extra goods go abroad. More and more, cheaper and cheaper.
scenes.text: More and more. | Cheaper and cheaper.

scenes.say: Exports rose 16 per cent in nine months.
scenes.label: Exports, January to September 2026, in yuan
scenes.speak: Exports rose sixteen per cent in nine months.

scenes.say: The trade surplus hit 938 billion dollars, after a record 1.2 trillion last year.
scenes.label: Trade surplus, January to September 2026
scenes.speak: The trade surplus hit nine hundred and thirty-eight billion dollars, after a record one point two trillion last year.

scenes.say: Selling abroad below fair value is called dumping.
From Europe to Asia, countries say it's killing their factories.
scenes.text: Europe to Asia: | it's killing our factories

scenes.say: India feels it directly. Last year it bought 131.6 billion dollars of goods from China, and sold it 19.5.
scenes.speak: India feels it directly. Last year it bought a hundred and thirty-one point six billion dollars of goods from China, and sold it nineteen point five.

scenes.say: A gap of about 112 billion dollars.
scenes.label: India's trade deficit with China, 2025-26
scenes.speak: A gap of about a hundred and twelve billion dollars.

scenes.say: India has opened a string of anti-dumping probes, from steel to drug ingredients.
scenes.title: Anti-dumping probes in 2026

scenes.say: India's only maker of penicillin G says it had to cut prices just to match Chinese imports.
Subsidies can pay for new factories. They can't set the price of imports.
scenes.text: Subsidies build plants. | They can't set prices.

scenes.say: Beijing knows the problem. Fixing it means shifting money from the state to households.
In July it set a target: 60 trillion yuan in retail sales by 2030.
scenes.label: Retail sales target for 2030, up from 50.1 trillion in 2025
scenes.speak: In July it set a target: sixty trillion yuan in retail sales by twenty-thirty.

scenes.say: It also promised to significantly raise household spending's share of the economy.
The IMF agrees.
scenes.text: "Transitioning to a consumption-led growth model should be the overarching priority."

scenes.say: But targets don't change how worried families spend.
For India, it cuts both ways.
If China's shoppers stay home, cheap imports keep coming.
If they start spending, China becomes a bigger market for India.
India's exports to China already rose by more than a third last year.
scenes.text: Exports to China: | up a third

scenes.say: China's spending gap is no longer just China's problem.
